title: Trace tables
specPoints: Interpret, correct or complete algorithms using **trace tables**
Determine the purpose of a simple algorithm by tracing it
Identify what a variable holds at each step
learn: Complete a trace table for an algorithm, one row per change
State the value each variable holds at any step
Work out the purpose of an algorithm by tracing it
Use a trace table to find where an algorithm goes wrong
hook: Here are six lines of code. Without running them, what does `x` equal at the end? Nobody is sure? That is normal — human brains are bad at holding several changing numbers at once. A trace table is a piece of paper that does the remembering for you, and it is worth up to 6 marks on Paper 2.

video.title: Trace tables: how to be a computer on paper
video.brief: 4 minutes. Show a 5-line loop that sums 1..4. Draw the table: one column per variable (i, total) plus an output column. Fill it row by row, one row per time a variable changes, highlighting the line being run. Pause at the loop condition each time. End with the two rules: a new row every time something changes; never work ahead in your head. Then show a second table with a deliberate bug (the loop stopping one early) and spot it from the table.

p: A **trace table** records the value of every variable each time the algorithm changes one. One column per variable, plus a column for any output and (optionally) one for the line number. You fill it in exactly as the computer would run the code — no shortcuts, no guessing.

list: Write a column for each variable you can see, and one for **Output**.
Start at the first line. Whenever a variable gets a value, write it in a **new row** under its column. Leave other cells blank (or copy down, if your teacher prefers).
At a loop or `if`, work out the condition **using the values in your table**, not in your head.
Keep going until the program ends. The last value in each column is the final state.
explain.code:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 3
    total = total + i
next i
print(total)

  i | total | Output
----+-------+-------
    |   0   |
  1 |   1   |
  2 |   3   |
  3 |   6   |
    |       |   6

explain.h: What exam questions do with trace tables
p: Three kinds: **complete** a partly filled table (the most common); **state the output** or **the final value** of a variable; and **state the purpose** of the algorithm. For purpose questions, look at what the output is in terms of the inputs: 'it outputs the largest of the numbers entered', 'it counts how many are over 50'. Describe the *job*, not the lines.

Working ahead and writing what you *think* it does; getting the loop boundary wrong (`for i = 1 to 3` runs with 1, 2 **and** 3); forgetting that `while` checks before the body; and missing the last row where the output happens. Slow is accurate.

simple.h: A table that remembers for you
p: A trace table is a table with one column for each variable and one for Output. You pretend to be the computer and write down every value as it changes.

list: One column per variable. One column for Output.
Run the code line by line. When a variable changes, write the new value in a new row.
At a loop or if, use the numbers **in the table** to decide.
simple.code:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 3
    total = total + i
next i
print(total)

  i | total | Output
----+-------+-------
    |   0   |
  1 |   1   |
  2 |   3   |
  3 |   6   |
    |       |   6

p: You might finish a table, say what the output is, or say what the algorithm is *for*. For 'what is it for', say the job: 'it adds up the numbers', 'it finds the biggest'.

keyterms.def: A table used to record the value of each variable, step by step, as an algorithm runs.
A named location in memory whose value can change while the program runs.
What the algorithm achieves overall, described in terms of its inputs and outputs.

try.title: 1. Complete the table
try.code:
x = 10
y = 3
while x > y
    x = x - y
    y = y + 1
endwhile
print(x)
steps: Draw columns for x, y, `x > y`, Output.
Fill it in. How many times does the loop body run?

try.title: 2. State the purpose
try.code:
nums = [4, 9, 2, 7]
big = nums[0]
for i = 1 to 3
    if nums[i] > big then
        big = nums[i]
    endif
next i
print(big)
steps: Trace it (columns: i, nums[i], big, Output).
Write one sentence: 'This algorithm …'. Do not mention variable names in the sentence.

try.title: 3. Find the bug with a trace
try.code:
count = 0
for i = 1 to 5
    if i MOD 2 == 0 then
        count = count + 1
    endif
next i
print("There are " + count + " odd numbers")
steps: Trace it. What does it actually count?
Fix the single character that is wrong, **or** fix the output message. Which fix is better and why?

try.title: 4. Check yourself in the pseudocode runner
instructions: Type Try 1 into the runner and add a `print(x, y)` inside the loop. Compare each printed pair with a row of your table.

check.q: In a trace table, when do you write a new row?
opts: Every time a variable changes value
check.fb: A row per change keeps the table honest.

check.q: `for i = 1 to 3` — how many rows will the i column have?
A trace of an algorithm shows it outputs the smallest input. The best statement of its purpose is:
opts: It uses a for loop and an if
It finds the minimum of a list of numbers
check.fb: Purpose is the job, in plain terms, without variable names.

check.q: In a `while` loop, where do you check the condition in your trace?
check.fb: `while` tests first, so it can run zero times.

check.q: Why should you not fill a trace table 'in your head'?
opts: You lose the method marks and make boundary errors
check.fb: Written working earns marks even if the final value slips.

exam.q: Complete the trace table for the algorithm below when the input is 23.
exam.code:
n = int(input())
count = 0
while n > 0
    n = n DIV 10
    count = count + 1
endwhile
print(count)
model: Rows: n 23, count 0 → n 2, count 1 → n 0, count 2 → loop stops; Output 2.
Marks: initial row (1), first iteration n=2 count=1 (1), second iteration n=0 count=2 (1), output 2 and no further rows (1).
exam.commentary: The trap is `DIV`: integer division, so 23 DIV 10 = 2, not 2.3. Students who write 2.3 then usually loop too many times. The second trap is an extra row after n becomes 0 — the condition is checked first and fails, so nothing else changes.

exam.q: State the purpose of the algorithm in the question above.
model: It counts the number of digits in the number entered (1).
exam.commentary: 'It divides by 10' describes a line, not the purpose. Marks need the overall job. If a student cannot see it, suggest trying a second input (e.g. 7 → 1, 450 → 3) and looking for the pattern.

exam.q: An algorithm is meant to output the average of five numbers entered. A trace shows it outputs the total instead. Explain what is missing.
model: The total is never divided by the number of values (1) — a line such as `average = total / 5` (or `/ count`) is needed before the output (1).
exam.commentary: Identify the error **and** give the fix. One without the other is one mark.

home: Write a 6-line algorithm of your own that uses a loop and one variable that changes. Swap with a partner (or hand it in). Trace each other's algorithm and state its purpose in one sentence.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 5 · explain 12 · try 25 · check 5 · exam 10 · homework 3
misconceptions: Working ahead mentally and writing the expected answer. Insist on the row-per-change rule.
`DIV` and `MOD` misread as ordinary division. Spend a minute on them before the exam task.
Inclusive `to` in `for` loops (again). Count the rows out loud.
Writing a purpose as a description of the code ('it loops and adds') rather than the job.
say: 'You are the computer. The computer doesn't know what the program is for. It just does the next line.'
'Point at the line you're on. Now point at the row you're writing. They should move together.'
'Purpose = what would you call this function if you had to name it?'
teacher.skip: Try 4 can go; the runner check is a confidence boost rather than a new skill.
differentiation: Support: give the trace table with the first two rows completed and the number of remaining rows indicated.
Stretch: write a trace for a nested loop (2 × 3) and predict the number of rows before starting.

pt.title: Tabelas de rastreio (trace tables)
pt.hook: Aqui estão seis linhas de código. Sem as executar, quanto vale `x` no fim? Ninguém tem a certeza? É normal — o cérebro humano é mau a guardar vários números que mudam ao mesmo tempo. Uma trace table é uma folha de papel que se lembra por ti, e vale até 6 marcas no Paper 2.

explain.h: O que é uma trace table
p: Uma **trace table** regista o valor de cada variável sempre que o algoritmo a altera. Uma coluna por variável, mais uma coluna para a saída (Output) e, opcionalmente, uma para o número da linha. Preenche-se exatamente como o computador executaria o código — sem atalhos, sem adivinhar.

list: Escreve uma coluna para cada variável e uma para **Output**.
Começa na primeira linha. Sempre que uma variável recebe um valor, escreve-o numa **nova linha** da tabela.
Num ciclo ou `if`, calcula a condição **com os valores da tabela**, não de cabeça.
Continua até o programa terminar. O último valor de cada coluna é o estado final.
explain.code:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 3
    total = total + i
next i
print(total)

  i | total | Output
----+-------+-------
    |   0   |
  1 |   1   |
  2 |   3   |
  3 |   6   |
    |       |   6

p: Três tipos: **completar** uma tabela parcialmente preenchida (o mais comum); **indicar a saída** ou **o valor final** de uma variável; e **indicar a finalidade** do algoritmo. Para a finalidade, olha para a saída em função das entradas: «dá o maior dos números introduzidos», «conta quantos estão acima de 50». Descreve o *trabalho*, não as linhas.

Avançar de cabeça e escrever o que *achas* que faz; errar o limite do ciclo (`for i = 1 to 3` corre com 1, 2 **e** 3); esquecer que o `while` testa antes do corpo; e falhar a última linha, onde acontece a saída. Devagar é certo.

keyterms.def: Tabela usada para registar o valor de cada variável, passo a passo, enquanto o algoritmo corre.
Um local com nome na memória cujo valor pode mudar durante a execução.
O que o algoritmo faz no seu todo, descrito em termos de entradas e saídas.
